item.title: Can We Grow After Disaster?
item.description:
Resilience

Can We Grow After Disaster?

Realistic optimism may shape resilience and growth after hardship.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Significant positive personal development and growth can happen after hardship.
  • Regulating emotions and adapting to challenges can help us navigate adversity.
  • Strong supportive relationships can be protective factors.

My mother used to tell the story of how, at the turn of the twentieth century, Han soldiers beheaded my great-grandfather in the middle of the street—there were large-scale massacres of Hui-Chinese people around the time of the Boxer Rebellion. After his death, my great-grandmother was seized and spent many years as the concubine of the village gunpowder maker. She wasn’t allowed an education or any means to earn a living. This was how the world worked then.

At the same time, the gunpowder maker did a few things that were decent and right. He owned a cow and asked my great-grandmother to milk it. She washed her hands, said a prayer, and sat on a wooden stool to soothe and coax the animal. The neighbors came by to fill their pails with milk and dropped their coins into the till. After the first milking, she handed the coins to the gunpowder maker.

He said, “The coins are yours.”

The next day, she milked the cow, accepted the neighbors’ coins, and handed them to the gunpowder maker. He said the same thing: “The coins are yours.” He said this day after day. Pocketing this money gave her faith and permission to dream. In the end, my great-grandmother bought her freedom with the coins. The cow was her saving grace; it gave her hope and resilience.

We had heard this story many times, and my sister added this notation in passing: “Hope is a good thing, but the right kind of hope is best. Don’t let that hope bleed into foolishness.” My sister was much wiser than most people.

Source: AI-Generated

Resilience is a highly useful ability to bounce back from hard times. It helps us face fears, reframe a glum view, regulate emotions, problem-solve, be flexible, and focus on what can be done, among other positive behaviors. Resilience protects us from what can beat us down. Resilient people can remain adaptable in the face of calamity and can sometimes even seem stronger than before a disaster.

The late Emmy Werner was among the earlier researchers to study this. She was a professor emerita at the University of California, Davis, and the author of many books, including Vulnerable But Invincible. She studied children on the Hawaiian island of Kauai and found that among the many children who were raised in adverse conditions, including insecure households and being in the care of mentally ill parents, about a third became competent and caring adults. What helped these individuals was strong bonds and connections with a kind and compassionate adult—a teacher, a relative, or a caretaker.

Growth After Disaster

Along with Werner and other researchers, psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, both at the University of North Carolina, have continued the study of psychological growth after a shocking disaster or failure, and they found that positive personal development can come about after adversity. Essentially, the proof is in the survivor. Someone who bravely fights cancer might feel she has been given extra time on Earth, and that sense of added time might help her gladly smell the roses. This phenomenon is called post-traumatic growth, in which the other side of trauma can lead survivors to change their perspectives, enhancing wisdom, gratitude, compassion, and generally focusing on what matters most in life.

However, some researchers, including psychologist Anthony Mancini of Pace University, wondered if such study results about post-traumatic growth have been accurate. Asking someone who has pulled through a catastrophe whether he is now a better person may be a flawed question. Often, studies use self-reported scales such as the Post-Traumatic Growth Inventory, which looks for positive responses in appreciation of life, relationships with others, new possibilities in life, personal strength, and spiritual change. However, self-reports may not be precise; Mancini has argued that a trauma survivor will certainly respond: Yes, I am a better person now.

But is the survivor really a better person as a result of surviving trauma? Perceived growth and actual growth may be two different things. A 2009 study in the journal Psychological Science reported that perceived growth and actual growth appear unrelated. Researchers learned that perceived growth is associated with increased distress from a trauma experienced, but actual growth is related to decreased distress. This may mean that perceived and actual growth each reflects different processes. Largely, a person may perceive that they are better and have improved after a trauma, but knowing that they actually are better is difficult. How would we know what the person was like before their traumatic event? Researchers like Mancini feel that self-reports may not always portray behavior accurately.

Arguably, if post-traumatic growth is just an illusion, I would rather have that illusion than feelings of no progress or hope. Sometimes a placebo effect does work.

A Hopeful View of Life

Surviving trauma does not promise a more positive mindset, but a survivor can bounce back from grave disappointment. While I have never lived through the hardship my great-grandma suffered, I did bounce back from strife. I want to be a hopeful and resilient person, one who sees the good in people. Those of us with a more hopeful personality seem to deliberate less and tend to avoid stewing over life’s petty annoyances. We may even try to find humor in situations.

My mother was well-practiced at telling me that the world did not notice how I pined for what could have been or might be in the future. She had no sympathy. The world did not rotate around me; she was sure of it. Of course, my sister always added, “Hey sis, the world just doesn’t care. Get over it.” I have taken this to heart. It actually helps me cope, even now.

There are ways to nurture hopeful thinking and resilience. One strategy is cognitive reappraisal, a technique used in cognitive behavioral and dialectical behavior therapies, among others. This entails reinterpreting an event or situation, which may involve expanding a viewpoint; such reframing may lead a person to more rational thinking. Instead of seeing something in a negative light, we can recalibrate our perspective and give it a hopeful and positive spin. There are ways to deploy this reappraisal.

We can use reflection to help ourselves reappraise events: “I wasn’t so sure about moving to my neighborhood at first, but I made friends and have a wonderful life now.” And flip the negative into a positive by using reappraisal as a learning tool: “That was a mistake; here’s how I can do better the next time.”

item.title: Do You Have to Forgive After Abuse?
item.description:
Forgiveness

Do You Have to Forgive After Abuse?

A trauma therapist explains why grief comes before forgiveness.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Many survivors of abuse feel pressure to forgive, often before they are ready.
  • Mourning and grief of what was lost has to come first, or forgiveness can prevent further healing.
  • Self-forgiveness is a critical first step in recovering from trauma and abuse.
Source: Anemone123/Pixabay

Survivors of domestic abuse are constantly told by society that they must forgive: “It’s for your own good; it will help you move on.” Especially for religious survivors who value the teachings of forgiveness from their place of worship. This can place a lot of weight on their shoulders.

Think about how unfair of a burden this places on the victim.

In my work with survivors of domestic abuse, I notice that many people return to therapy after a few months or even years believing they were OK, thinking that they “forgave” the person who hurt them but arriving at the same pain and grief as before. I believe this is because they never fully allowed themself to acknowledge, mourn, and heal from their grief.

Work on trauma in the mental health community teaches us that mourning needs to happen following trauma—mourning for the loss of love and expectations of a relationship, dignity and pride, grief, and embarrassment. Instead of mourning, many survivors find themselves in an extended period of denial. They do this by convincing themselves that they were in an OK place because they had chosen to forgive, falsely giving them the assumption that they have finished and moved past the experience.

Thorough and complete mourning is necessary to move on from trauma.

Mourning will be a unique process for every survivor, but I have several techniques to help you along the way. Following these tricks can incorporate space for healing into your recovery.

1. First, forgive yourself

With all of the pressure for survivors to forgive others, I frequently reflect that back on them. Survivors of trauma place a lot of guilt and blame on themselves for having gone through an abusive experience. Maybe they think they broke their partner’s heart, fought too much, worked too many late nights, or came home irritable too often. It is possible to share responsibility for the flaws in a relationship that caused it to fail without being responsible for any of the malicious actions at the hands of your ex-partner. There is a difference between malicious cruelty and the everyday flaws and shortcomings we all exhibit. Forgive yourself for not seeing red flags and “getting away sooner.” Forgive yourself for what your children saw. And forgive yourself for waiting too long to seek legal support and forgive yourself for any legal repercussions that the perpetrator ends up with. None of this is your fault.

2. Remind yourself that you have a right to love

A lot of the blame for LGBTQ individuals might come from simply being a member of a marginalized community. Religious or conservative upbringings might have taught them to believe that existing within this community of love is a “sin” worthy of its due punishment. Many of my patients have expressed such thoughts. Their abuse was punishment for being gay, queer, trans, or other places on the love spectrum outside of where society says they “should” exist. This guilt stays with them unless it can be resolved at the source. Their mourning will often start with accepting who they are and the fact that they have a right to love. That their love is not a sin and that in no way do they deserve to be punished for it.

3. Keep a journal

I recommend this at every stage of the recovery process. When we look back at our writing long after experiencing the trauma firsthand, we can see our growth written in our words. Once you can feel safe enough to express your feelings and mourn in a supportive environment, this natural progression will happen inside of you. Keeping a journal will provide you with this tangible evidence of how far you have made it from the fear and pain of your abuse.

It is important to understand that healing is not linear. Remember, you will have good days and bad days. Good hours may be followed by a bad hour. It is normal and natural to have different emotional reactions with varying degrees of severity as you move forward.

Forgiveness is a personal choice, not a requirement for healing. If forgiveness comes one day, let it come because it feels authentic—not because someone else told you it was necessary. Until then, give yourself permission to grieve what was lost, to forgive yourself, and to heal at your own pace.

Excerpted, in part, from my book Invisible Bruises: How a Better Understanding of the Patterns of Domestic Violence Can Help Survivors Navigate the Legal System.

item.title: Love and Resentment: Why They Coexist in Close Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Love and Resentment: Why They Coexist in Close Relationships

If only love and resentment were mutually exclusive.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Resentment works like ice on a wound; it numbs pain but prevents healing.
  • To escape the chronic reactivity that resentment engenders, behave in ways that make you like yourself better.
  • Blame can turn hidden guilt and shame into resentment.

Though understandable and usually justified, resentment is a self-eroding emotional state that makes us powerless over our own well-being. Instead of improving, it makes us devalue someone else, keeping us in enduring devalued states. It works like ice on a wound, numbing pain but preventing healing. It impairs self-awareness and turns us into someone we’re not. We cannot heal and resent at the same time.

Resentment impairs self-awareness because it feels different from the way it looks. We may feel hurt or mistreated but look mean and unfriendly—in facial expressions, body tension, tone of voice. People respond to how we look, not how we feel.

Resentment turns us into reactaholics, unsure of what we think and feel, unless we’re negatively reacting to someone or something.

Reacting is easy, but acting in your long-term best interest is not. Our brains are short-term oriented, replete with tacit judgments and habituated responses to environmental conditions. If judgments and habits violate deeper values, we’ll fall prey to chronic reactivity. We’ll react to jerks like a jerk, accuse when we feel accused, manipulate when we feel manipulated, try to silence when we feel unheard, shame others when feeling shame.

To escape the yoke of reactivity that resentment engenders, behave in ways that will let you like yourself better.

Engines of Resentment

Hidden guilt and shame permeate our lives. We’re rarely aware of them, due to well-honed defenses against them, mostly blame, denial, and avoidance, which produce resentment.

Most unconscious guilt and shame rise from violating our own values. But they are not punishments; they’re motivations to honor our values. That functional motivation is obviated by blaming others.

Relationship Warnings

Red flags include partners getting irritated by things they used to like, including facial and verbal expressions, laughter, or dress. They're often less intimate—reduced talking, touch, hugging, eye contact, sharing experience, and sex. They judge each other’s perspectives with no interest in learning about them. They’re annoyed by each other’s feelings and intolerant of differences.

Decline of attachment emotions (interest, trust, compassion, love) automatically increases resentment. Reinvesting interest, trust, compassion, and love automatically reduces resentment.

On our deathbeds, we won’t think about our partners not appreciating us enough but we’ll likely regret not sufficiently appreciating our partners. When we die and go to judgment, they won’t ask us what our partners did.

Resentment fades when we try to improve situations and experiences instead of blaming them on loved ones.

Think Healing, Not Forgiveness

A healing identity is focused on resilience, strengths, and capacity to sympathize with and heal our hurt. It's the opposite of victim identity, which emphasizes damage and bad things that have happened to us or that will happen to us. We outgrow victim identity as we build more value, appreciation, humanity, and meaning in our lives.

Most forgiveness occurs as a byproduct of healing, rather than a cause of it. We heal and then forgive, not the other way around. Attempting to forgive while in pain is like trying to put out an oilfield fire without sealing the wells.

Genuine, lasting forgiveness is a byproduct of compassion—both giving it and receiving it.
